That is deliberate: for this subject the PD material is better than anything a
permissive-but-modern search turns up, so there is no reason to take on a
Two kinds of picture, and the difference is the point. A nineteenth-century
painting of the Ides of March is a Roman scene imagined by a Roman-obsessed
age, not evidence. A coin struck in 29 BC and the Res Gestae cut into a temple
wall ARE evidence, and the chapters say so where they use them. The credit
line under every plate gives the artist and the year, so a reader can see
whether they are looking at 1805 or at 44 BC.
Where the object is ancient but the photograph is not, the photograph carries
its own licence. CC BY-SA is fine and credited automatically; NC is not, and
would make the whole build non-commercial. Read the licence, not a summary.
